parts.text: Burning or fissioning a fuel to generate electricity inefficiently, transmitting it far away, and turning it back into

heat for homes was “like cutting butter with a chainsaw,” Lovins wrote. Thus, his soft path included only a narrowing lane for electricity, steering it toward essential purposes such as electronics, subways, lighting and smelting. Lovins posited that “an

industrial economy could advantageously operate with no central power stations at all,” though he did not advocate going that far.

The road taken

They were paths, not predictions, and neither path foretold the road actually taken in the 50 years since. Unlike most

from the era, which projected ever-rising demand, the soft path foresaw that total U.S. energy use could plateau, and it almost exactly matched the actual level in 2000. However, Lovins and his contemporaries failed to foresee the

advances that have kept oil and gas dominant.

As an environmental engineer completing a book about the visions that are shaping energy realities and opportunities around the world, I think Lovins got it half right about how to secure

energy. Efficiency and renewable energy are indeed essential, but clean electricity and electrification are proving far more important than Lovins expected.

Critics argued that Lovins underestimated the costs of clean technologies and

what they could achieve. In fact, opportunities for clean energy have been transformed by unanticipated plunges in the costs of wind and solar electricity, battery storage and LED lighting.

For example, the price per watt of solar panels

from around US$100 in current dollars in 1976 to around 10 cents in global markets today and a President Donald Trump-set minimum price of 38 cents for panels imported to the United States.

The soft path goes electric

Modern technologies turn the chainsaw

on its head by making electrification the soft path to reducing energy use. Heat pumps supply several times as much heat as the electricity they consume. Induction stoves cook food far more efficiently than gas flames. And electric vehicles are a few times more

than gasoline ones.

Powered by renewable electricity, from local resources like the solar panels on Lovins’ roof and mine, or from larger solar, wind and geothermal facilities, these technologies can slash fossil fuel use. A
of resources blended with high-voltage transmission and storage can make clean electricity available around the clock.
